newsitem.title: TURKEY: Erbakan says Turkey to be treated with respect.
newsitem.headline: Erbakan says Turkey to be treated with respect.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan on Tuesday said ahead of a visit by German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel that Turkey should be treated with more respect internationally.
"It will be very interesting to meet with him (Kinkel). Now nobody can give Turkey the 'do this, do that' treatment," he told a meeting of MPs from his Islamist Welfare Party.
"The respect and treatment which the new world leader Turkey deserves will be realised," he said.
Kinkel arrives in Ankara on Tuesday evening and will meet Erbakan and Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller on Wednesday. He goes to Istanbul on Thursday.
During his visit Kinkel is expected to try to appease NATO ally Turkey over the continued European Union rejection of Ankara's long-standing bid to join the bloc.

Europe's Christian Democrat leaders, including Germany's Chancellor Helmut Kohl, said earlier this month that Turkey's Moslem culture made it unfit to join the EU. Kinkel and other EU foreign ministers have distanced themselves from these statements.
Erbakan said Turkey had incurred losses because of a customs accord with the EU that went into effect at the start of 1996.

"There will be a $5 billion loss for Turkey because it has entered the customs union...After they have done this they will bow their heads when they talk with Turkey," Erbakan told the Welfare Party meeting.

EU exports to Turkey have surged under the accord while Turkish exports to the bloc have changed little. Millions of dollars in EU transitonal aid have been blocked by Greece over disputes in Cyprus and the Aegean and by EU states concerned about Ankara's human rights record.
Turkey has been an associate member of the EU since 1963 and regards it unjust that other states, including former eastern bloc adversaries, might get into the EU before Ankara.
But some European leaders fear that distancing Turkey from Europe could lead the country, overwhelmingly Moslem but officially secular, to turn toward other Moslem countries instead.
